Today in the corridor I waved at Farhan and called his name. He looked at me for one second and then turned his whole body away and walked off toward the lab.
I stood there with my hand still up like an idiot. Two people saw.

In the Chandigarh community hall, the district chess final was about to start. Vaibhav sat at the board, and his shoulders had crept up almost to his ears. His neck felt stiff.
His coach, Gurleen Ma'am, tapped him lightly. "Shoulders."
"What about them?"

"Every time you're thinking hard, check them," Ma'am said.

Tonight I asked Tenzin how school was. He shrugged, eyes on his plate. I asked if he'd had a test. Another shrug. I felt annoyed. It looked like he didn't care.
Later, driving to the chemist, I tried again, but differently. "What was the best part of your day, and the worst?"

In Class 9, when Sonali presented her science project, I made air quotes and said, "Her 'amazing' project." Everyone laughed.
I thought it was funny. But Sonali's face dropped. She finished her presentation, but her voice was shaky.
Later, she came up to me. "Why did you do that? I worked on it for two weeks."
I felt terrible. I said sorry. I told her I didn't think about how it would feel.
Now when I use air quotes, I think first. They can make a joke, but they can also make someone feel small.
- Kunal

qa.q: How long did Sonali work on her project?
qa.a: Two weeks.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling when Kunal made air quotes?
qa.a: Sonali felt hurt and embarrassed, since the air quotes mocked her hard work.

qa.q: What did Kunal learn to do differently?
qa.a: Kunal learned to think before using air quotes, because they can put someone down.

qa.q: How might the classmates who laughed see the air quotes now?
qa.a: They might realise the air quotes were a put-down, not just a joke.

grounding: The narrator recalls using air quotes to mock a classmate's project and learning that tone decides if they are teasing or hurtful.

Teacher's note, Monday
When I assigned the weekend essay, Shankar stood up and gave me a big mock salute. "Yes, ma'am!" Everyone laughed, including me. His grin was friendly, and he started the essay right away.
Later, though, when Priyanka shared her idea for the class trip, Shankar made air quotes: "'Great' idea." Priyanka went quiet.
I spoke to him after class. I told him the salute was funny because it was friendly, but the air quotes felt like a put-down.
He looked surprised. "I was joking."
"It didn't feel like a joke to Priyanka," I said.
Tomorrow he's going to talk to her.
- Ms Devika

qa.q: What did Shankar say when he saluted?
qa.a: "Yes, ma'am!"

qa.q: What was Priyanka feeling when Shankar made air quotes?
qa.a: Priyanka felt hurt and embarrassed, reading the air quotes as mockery of her idea.

qa.q: What did Ms Devika do that helped?
qa.a: She pointed out the difference in tone between the friendly salute and the mocking air quotes, and encouraged Shankar to talk to Priyanka.

qa.q: How might Shankar see his own gestures after the talk?
qa.a: Shankar might realise that even jokes can hurt, depending on tone and who they're aimed at.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a teenager using a friendly mock salute and hurtful air quotes, showing tone decides the meaning.

passage:
Friday
I won the inter-school debate today!! My hands were still shaking from the last rebuttal when I came off stage. Jahnavi was waiting at the steps and gave me a big, slow, serious salute, then burst out grinning. It felt like she was really proud of me, like I was a general coming back from battle.
But then in the canteen, someone from the other team said, "Here comes the 'winner,'" doing air quotes. My stomach dropped.
Jahnavi saw my face. She said loudly, "Yes, the real winner," and saluted again.
I laughed, and the knot in my stomach went away. Same kind of gesture, both done with fingers in the air, but one was a put-down and one was respect. It all depends on the face and the voice that come with it.
- Jaya

qa.q: What did Jahnavi do when Jaya came off stage?
qa.a: She gave a big salute, grinning.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling when the other team used air quotes?
qa.a: Jaya felt hurt and deflated, since the air quotes made the win seem fake.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi do that helped?
qa.a: Jahnavi countered the put-down by saying "the real winner" and saluting again, showing respect.

qa.q: How might the student from the other team have seen the air quotes?
qa.a: They may have been disappointed about losing and used the air quotes to feel better, not caring how it hurt.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows a friendly salute as respect and air quotes as a put-down, with tone deciding meaning.

passage:
Yesterday my brother Lalit had an argument over a cricket game with a boy from the next lane. As we walked home, the boy rode past on his bike and flashed the middle finger right at Lalit.
Lalit's jaw went tight, and his hands clenched. I thought he'd shout back. But he took a breath, stepped back onto the footpath, and kept walking with me.
"That boy did the same last week," he muttered.
When we got home, Lalit told Papa everything. Papa listened and said he'd speak to the boy's parents that evening, and that Lalit had done the right thing by staying calm.
I don't know if Lalit was angry or scared. Probably both.
- Lavanya

qa.q: What did the boy on the bike do?
qa.a: He flashed the middle finger right at Lalit.

qa.q: What might Lalit have been feeling when his hands clenched?
qa.a: Lalit was likely angry and possibly scared, but he chose to stay calm; Lavanya can't be sure which feeling was stronger.

qa.q: What did Lalit do that was safe and wise?
qa.a: He stepped back, stayed calm, and told Papa the same day, since it had happened before.

qa.q: How did Papa respond to Lalit?
qa.a: Papa listened, praised him for staying calm, and planned to speak to the boy's parents that evening.

grounding: An observer sees a teenager recognise a rude gesture as an insult, step back calmly, and tell an adult since it came from ongoing bullying.

passage:
"Lalremsiami, you want to know why I never make rude gestures, even in traffic? Let me, your Zeenat Aunty, tell you.
When I was fifteen, I was late for the school bus, and the driver drove off without me. I was so angry, I raised my middle finger at the bus as it left.
The next day, the driver told the principal. I was banned from the bus for a week. My father had to drive me every day, and I had to apologise to the driver in front of everyone.
I felt so ashamed. The driver hadn't done anything wrong. I'd just been late.
Rude gestures might feel good for a second, but they hurt people and they come back to you."

qa.q: How long was Zeenat banned from the bus?
qa.a: A week.

qa.q: What was young Zeenat feeling when she apologised to the driver?
qa.a: She felt ashamed, knowing the driver had done nothing wrong and she had been late.

qa.q: What choice inside the story led to the consequence?
qa.a: Zeenat's choice to raise her middle finger at the bus led to the ban and the public apology.

qa.q: How might the bus driver have felt seeing the gesture?
qa.a: The driver probably felt insulted and hurt, since he had only been doing his job.

grounding: An aunt recalls using a rude gesture as a teenager and the real consequences, showing such gestures hurt others.

passage:
Dear Kashish Ma'am,
I wanted to explain about today's online class. When you asked me a question, I didn't answer for a long time. I know it looked like I wasn't paying attention.
Actually, my internet was lagging, and your voice kept cutting out. I clicked the raise-hand button twice, but I don't think it showed on your screen.
Also, I get really shy speaking on video. When everyone's camera is on and it's silent, I freeze.
Could I type my answers in the chat sometimes? Or use the hand emoji when I want to talk?
Thank you for understanding.
Varun

qa.q: How many times did Varun click the raise-hand button?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling during the silence in the online class?
qa.a: Varun felt shy and frozen speaking on video, and frustrated by the lag.

qa.q: What did Varun suggest to make online class easier?
qa.a: Typing answers in the chat or using the hand emoji when wanting to talk.

qa.q: How might Kashish Ma'am have seen Varun's silence before the email?
qa.a: Kashish Ma'am might have thought Varun wasn't paying attention, not knowing about the lag and shyness.

grounding: In an email, a teenager explains silence in an online class as lag and shyness, and suggests digital tools to take turns.

passage:
"Imran, you know how online classes were? For me, the mute button was my best friend. I'd keep it on unless I had something to say.
But one day, Mr Ghosh asked me something, and I didn't answer. I was trying to unmute, but my laptop froze. He said, 'Rajni, if you're not interested, you can leave.' My face went hot.
After class, I emailed him. I said my laptop froze, and I had clicked the raise-hand button. He wrote back, 'Sorry. I couldn't tell on my side.'
After that, he started saying, 'If you're stuck, type a hand emoji in the chat.' So now I, Rajni, use the hand emoji every time."

qa.q: What did Mr Ghosh say to Rajni when the answer didn't come?
qa.a: "Rajni, if you're not interested, you can leave."

qa.q: What was Rajni feeling when Mr Ghosh spoke to her like that?
qa.a: Rajni felt embarrassed and hurt, since the silence was because the laptop froze, not lack of interest.

qa.q: What did Rajni do that helped?
qa.a: Rajni emailed Mr Ghosh to explain, which led him to suggest using a hand emoji in the chat.

qa.q: How might Mr Ghosh see silence in video calls after Rajni's email?
qa.a: He might realise silence can mean technical problems, not lack of interest.

grounding: A teenager tells a friend how silence in an online class was misread as disinterest, and how digital tools helped.

passage:
My sister Binita's online class was on in the next room. Her camera was off, and I could see her through the doorway, sitting very still.
Then the teacher said, "Binita? Are you there?"
She didn't answer at first. I thought maybe she wasn't paying attention.
Then I saw her fingers flying on the keyboard. She typed "🙋 Sorry, lagging!" in the chat. A few seconds later, she unmuted and answered the question.
Later I asked her why she didn't just talk. She said, "Sometimes the sound cuts out, and I don't want to talk over someone."
I didn't know silence in online class could mean so many things.
- Chetan

qa.q: What did Binita type in the chat?
qa.a: "🙋 Sorry, lagging!"

qa.q: What might Binita have been feeling when the teacher called her name?
qa.a: She may have felt anxious and flustered, waiting for the lag to clear before she could answer.

qa.q: What did Binita do to take her turn without speaking over others?
qa.a: She used the chat and a hand emoji to show she was there before unmuting.

qa.q: How did Chetan see the silence at first?
qa.a: Chetan thought Binita wasn't paying attention, not realising it was lag.

grounding: An observer sees a teenager use a chat emoji to take a turn in an online class, learning silence can mean lag.
